title: Mansa Musa and the gold nobody could count
subtitle: A king from Mali set out for Mecca in 1324 and drew the attention of the Muslim world. How much of the story is record, and how much is legend?

sections.title: A journey that put Mali on the map

parts.text: In 1324 Mansa Musa, a devout Muslim, set off on pilgrimage to Mecca.
The route taken by the ruler and his entourage in 1324–25 covered over 4,000 miles.

items.text: The reign of Mansa Musa, emperor of Mali.
Al-Umari records the account of Musa's visit to Cairo.

parts.text: An Arab writer reported that he travelled with 20,000 people and more than 2,000 pounds of gold.
Other retellings give other totals, so none of them is a measurement.

blocks.prompt: By one estimate, what share of the world's gold supply did Musa's Mali control?

parts.text: An estimated half, according to South African History Online, a weaker source.
A Smithsonian podcast says he is said to have been the richest man ever.
A 2026 fact-check says economic historians agree his wealth cannot be pinned to a number, and traces the figure of $400 billion to a 2012 website list.
The $400 billion figure traces to a 2012 website list, not to a medieval source.

blocks.q: Myth or fact: Mansa Musa was certainly the richest person who ever lived.
blocks.explain: A 2026 fact-check says economic historians agree his wealth cannot be pinned to a number, and the Smithsonian podcast only says he is 'said to have been' the richest.

parts.text: The British Museum says that Mali's power and wealth came from trading gold and salt, including through the city of Timbuktu.
The geographer Ibn Hawqal wrote that the king of Ghana was 'the wealthiest king on the face of the earth'; the page dates this to 951, though other sources say about 977.
So the idea of a fabulously rich West African king is older than Musa by more than three centuries.
Al-Umari wrote that Musa left no court emir and no holder of a royal office without the gift of a load of gold.
Al-Umari also reported that the price of gold in Cairo fell: the mithqal, which had not gone below 25 dirhams, afterwards did not exceed 22, and this had lasted about twelve years.
Other sources give the length of the fall as between ten and twelve years, or about ten.
How large and lasting the fall really was is a question for the specialist literature, which this page has not read.

blocks.q: According to al-Umari, how long had gold stayed at the lower price in Cairo?
blocks.explain: Al-Umari's account, as printed in Levtzion and Hopkins, says this had been the state of affairs for about twelve years.

sections.title: How we know what we know

parts.text: Al-Umari recorded the account about a decade after the visit.
His text is printed in the Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History, by Levtzion and Hopkins (1981).
Much of what we know therefore reaches us through Arabic writers. Mali's own oral tradition is not represented in the sources read for this page, so the story here is the record's, not Mali's.

gaps: Left out because no readable source outside Wikipedia supported them: the figure of 2,700 miles, the three days at the Pyramids, the three months in Cairo and the departure on 18 October, the two thirds of Mediterranean gold, Bambuk and Bure as the gold fields, the two seventeenth-century Timbuktu chronicles, and the date of 1337 for his death.
The Metropolitan Museum pages on the trans-Saharan gold trade could not be opened (error 429) and are not cited.
Warren Schultz's 2006 article on the price of gold in Cairo, and Levtzion and Hopkins's Corpus itself, were not read directly; the account here comes from extracts.
Ibn Hawqal's date differs between sources (951 on the page used, about 977 elsewhere).
Two sources used, South African History Online and a fact-check on Ancient Origins, are weaker and marked 'to verify'.

keyPoints.text: In 1324 Mansa Musa set off on pilgrimage to Mecca; the route of 1324–25 covered over 4,000 miles.
An Arab writer reported 20,000 people and more than 2,000 pounds of gold; the numbers cannot be treated as a count.
Al-Umari wrote that the price of gold in Cairo stayed low for about twelve years after the visit.
Economic historians agree his wealth cannot be pinned to a number, says a recent fact-check.
